quote:
- Current suicidal intent, new plan, access to lethal means, or sudden worsening.
- Threats toward others or escalating agitation.
problem: The packet's 'escalate immediately' list sets the student's reporting threshold at intent/plan/means for suicide and at 'threats' for violence; it does not tell a student what to do when a patient discloses suicidal thoughts without stated intent, or homicidal thoughts about a person without an overt threat. The companion Interview & MSE pocket guide sets the correct, lower threshold ('A positive answer anywhere above goes to your resident or attending now').
whyItMatters: An MS3 who cannot yet judge intent reliably may sit on a disclosure of passive or active SI, or of HI toward a named person, until rounds because it 'did not meet' the listed criteria; judging intent and deciding on duty-to-protect steps belong to the supervisor, not the student.
evidence: Internal inconsistency with pg_interview.md ('A positive answer anywhere above goes to your resident or attending now, not at the end of the day — the disposition call is theirs'); Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01 (a positive screen triggers clinician assessment); duty-to-protect statutes differ by state and depend on identifying a victim, which is a supervisor-level decision.
correction:
- Any new or newly disclosed suicidal thoughts (even passive or without a plan), current suicidal intent, new plan, preparatory behavior, access to lethal means, or sudden worsening.
- Thoughts of harming or killing someone (especially a named person), threats toward others, or escalating agitation.
verified: recall; cross-checked against pg_interview.md in this chunk

quote: Escalate immediately for: current suicidal intent or new plan, threats or escalating agitation
problem: The key-point card sets the escalation threshold at intent/new plan and 'threats'. It leaves out any disclosure of suicidal thoughts without intent and any homicidal ideation that has not been voiced as a threat.
whyItMatters: The card is shown without the page's context. A student may take it to mean that SI or HI short of intent or threat can wait for rounds, which contradicts the pocket guide's 'any positive answer goes now' rule.
evidence: pg_interview.md in this chunk: 'A positive answer anywhere above goes to your resident or attending now'.
correction: Escalate immediately for: any new suicidal or homicidal thoughts, current suicidal intent or new plan, threats or escalating agitation

quote: Escalate current intent, preparatory behavior, means access, intoxication/withdrawal, severe agitation, psychosis, or contradictory collateral.
problem: The required Week 1 safety set tells students to ask directly about suicidal thoughts, but its escalation list begins at intent. It does not say that a disclosure of suicidal (or homicidal) thoughts by itself must go to the resident. There is also no homicidal-ideation item anywhere in the Week 1 set: the agitation bullet covers threats and behavior, not a disclosed wish to kill someone.
whyItMatters: In their first week, students may conclude that ideation without stated intent is theirs to hold. They are not yet competent to decide that.
evidence: pg_interview.md in this chunk ('A positive answer anywhere above goes to your resident or attending now … the disposition call is theirs').
correction: Tell the resident the same encounter about any new suicidal or homicidal thoughts, and escalate immediately for current intent, preparatory behavior, means access, intoxication/withdrawal, severe agitation, psychosis, or contradictory collateral.

quote: the screen is diagnostic and the lorazepam challenge can be therapeutic
problem: This sentence has the roles backwards. The Bush-Francis screening items (the first 14; positive if 2 or more) are a screen, not a diagnosis. The lorazepam challenge is the diagnostic test (a response supports catatonia), and it is also the start of treatment.
whyItMatters: A student may record catatonia as diagnosed on the strength of a positive screen, skipping the DSM-5-TR criteria (3 of 12 features) and the medical workup. Or they may not realise that a negative or partial lorazepam response carries diagnostic weight.
evidence: Bush G et al., Acta Psychiatr Scand 1996;93:129-136 (BFCSI: 14-item screen, 2+ items positive; the lorazepam challenge confirmed the diagnosis in most cases); DSM-5-TR catatonia criteria (3 or more of 12 psychomotor features).
correction: a positive screen prompts a supervised diagnostic assessment, and a lorazepam challenge both supports the diagnosis and begins treatment

quote: Rosenhan 1973 (labeling), and Appelbaum & Grisso 1988 (capacity) — three papers that shape
problem: Rosenhan's 'On being sane in insane places' is recommended as a landmark with no caveat. Archival investigations since 2019 have documented serious evidence that the data were misreported or fabricated (for example, missing pseudopatients and an excluded participant whose experience contradicted the thesis).
whyItMatters: Students on a national curriculum will cite this study as evidence that psychiatric diagnosis cannot tell the sane from the insane, a claim its own records do not support.
evidence: Scull A. 'Rosenhan revisited: successful scientific fraud.' Hist Psychiatry 2023 (PMID 36737877); Cahalan S. The Great Pretender (2019).
correction: Rosenhan 1973 (labeling — read with Scull 2023, which documents serious doubts about its data), and Appelbaum & Grisso 1988 (capacity) — three papers that shape

problem: The page text repeats the overlay: Rosenhan 1973 appears as suggested reading with no note of the documented concerns about its data.
whyItMatters: Fixing only the overlay card would leave the page text recommending the study without a caveat.
correction: **Suggested reading:** Engel 1977 (biopsychosocial) · Rosenhan 1973 (labeling; read with Scull 2023 on the study's contested data) · Appelbaum & Grisso 1988 (capacity).

quote: | 5 | Acute/consult psychiatry deep practice | Formulate suicide/violence risk, recognize delirium/catatonia/withdrawal, and document supervised escalation reasoning |
problem: The weekly skill map places suicide and violence risk formulation in Week 5. Yet students are asked to give a 'risk update' in every presentation from Day 1, to request feedback on whether their risk formulation 'separates chronic and acute risk', and to complete a supervised Stanley-Brown safety plan with a patient in Week 3, which presupposes a risk formulation.
whyItMatters: Students may treat risk formulation as late-rotation content, and so build safety plans and daily risk updates for four weeks without the formulation the plan is meant to address.
evidence: Internal: orientation.md 'Risk update' and feedback prompts; week3.md overlay (supervised safety plan in Week 3); Stanley & Brown 2012, Cogn Behav Pract (the safety plan follows the risk assessment).
correction: | 5 | Acute/consult psychiatry deep practice | Deepen the suicide/violence risk formulation practised since Week 1 (and used for Week 3 safety planning), recognize delirium/catatonia/withdrawal, and document supervised escalation reasoning |

quote: | 3 | Treatment | Explain why a medication and one non-medication intervention fit the formulation |
problem: The packet's week map does not match the shipped week pages. The Compass and week2.md put pharmacology in Week 2 ('Mood, Psychosis & Pharm'). Week 3 is Psychotherapy & Personality, with supervised safety planning as its skill of the week.
whyItMatters: Students preparing from the packet will look for pharmacology and safety-planning work in the wrong week.
evidence: Internal: welcome.md Compass and week2.md / week3.md in this chunk.
correction: | 3 | Psychotherapy, personality, safety planning | Explain why one non-medication intervention fits the formulation and complete a supervised collaborative safety plan |

quote: Efficacy differences are small; the side-effect profile is what you are actually choosing.
problem: Stated without qualification, this leaves out clozapine, whose superior efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia was shown in CATIE's own Phase 2E and in later network meta-analyses. The same absolute framing appears in the overlay ('not by generation') and in the reflection ('pick by profile, not class').
whyItMatters: A student may conclude that after two failed antipsychotic trials, switching to a third agent chosen by side-effect profile is equivalent to clozapine. That delays the one evidence-based treatment for treatment resistance.
evidence: McEvoy JP et al., CATIE Phase 2E, Am J Psychiatry 2006;163:600-610 (clozapine more effective than switching to another atypical); Leucht S et al., Lancet 2013 network meta-analysis; APA Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia 2020 (clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia).
correction: Efficacy differences are small (except clozapine for treatment-resistant illness); the side-effect profile is what you are usually choosing.

quote: Always document suicidal and homicidal ideation explicitly — including their absence. "Denies SI/HI" is not optional.
problem: The tool presents 'Denies SI/HI' as the required documentation. The companion pocket guide in the same chunk warns against exactly that shorthand: its words-to-use-carefully list says '"Denies" alone -> include what you asked and how risk was reasoned', and its can't-miss card says '"Denies SI/HI — no risk" is not a risk assessment'.
whyItMatters: Students will write 'denies SI/HI' as their whole safety record, without the questions asked or collateral findings. That kind of note fails to show an assessment took place.
evidence: Internal conflict with pg_interview.md; Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01 EP 2-3 (screening with a validated tool followed by evidence-based assessment, documented).
correction: Always document suicidal and homicidal ideation explicitly — including their absence, with what you asked (e.g., "denies SI/HI when asked directly about thoughts, plan, and recent steps").
